newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean chides Russia on "space garbage".
newsitem.headline: Chilean chides Russia on "space garbage".

text.p: Chile's defence minister said Russia owed Chile an explanation as to why it took so long to inform Santiago about a Russian space probe that crashed in the ocean near Chile with 12 ounces (200 grams) of plutonium on board.
Calling the satellite "space garbage," Defence Minister Edmundo Perez Yoma said the Russian government told Chile of the incident at the same time it told the rest of the world.

"The Russian authorities have an information policy that we, at least, don't completely understand," he told reporters. "We were informed ... with some delay by the authorities, and that needs to be clarified."
Any formal protest to Moscow would have to come from the Chilean Foreign Ministry, said Perez Yoma.

Chilean officials were apparently caught completely unaware by the crash on Sunday of the Mars 96 probe in the South Pacific about 720 nautical miles from Chile's Easter Island. Early reports had suggested it would hit Earth somewhere in Australia.

"It's difficult to make any warnings when it's an accident," said Perez Yoma. "But of course this is not very welcome for the countries that receive this space garbage, and we will make our point of view known to prevent this (in the future)."
The Mars 96 probe, which blasted off on Saturday, fell back to Earth the next day after it failed to break out of the Earth's gravitational field when a rocket misfired.
The satellite first looked as if it would crash on Australia, but overshot it and plunged instead into the Pacific between Easter Island and the Chilean mainland, scientists said.

Most of the satellite burned up on re-entry but some of it probably survived, including four tiny canisters containing enough plutonium to cause hundreds of cases of cancer if it came in contact with people, U.S. scientists said.
Officials reassured Chileans they had nothing to fear from the accident, which apparently left the highly radioactive plutonium 6,000 yards (meters) down at the ocean bottom.
Chilean officials have said the remains are too deep to recover and they saw no danger to the public from the plutonium, which was packed to withstand great pressure.
Fernandez said that any radiation from the accident would be tiny in comparison to that released in French atomic tests in the South Pacific last year.
